genZNote: Catalase negative, cheese-industry royalty, and about as far from a hospital pathogen as a Gram-positive coccus gets.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Plant surfaces and raw milk; historically classified under 'Streptococcus lactis' before reclassification
habitat.hostAssociation: Not a normal human commensal — essentially non-pathogenic
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Used worldwide as a starter culture for cheese, buttermilk, and other fermented dairy products
habitat.reservoir: Plants and dairy environments rather than an animal/human reservoir

microscopy.appearance: Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains

culture.media: M17 agar (industrial dairy microbiology) or standard blood agar
culture.colonyMorphology: Small, smooth, white to gray colonies

identificationClues: Central organism in cheese and buttermilk fermentation (converts lactose to lactic acid)
Almost never recovered as a clinical pathogen

diseases: Essentially non-pathogenic; rare case reports of opportunistic bacteremia/endocarditis in patients with significant comorbidities
clinicalImportance.transmission: Not a human-to-human pathogen — encountered via food fermentation, not infection
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the most industrially important bacteria in the world via cheese, yogurt-adjacent, and buttermilk production; also a widely used genetic model organism for lactic acid bacteria
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: A catalase-negative Gram-positive coccus recovered from a clinical specimen should prompt consideration of viridans streptococci/enterococci first, given how rarely Lactococcus causes disease

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Catalase negative; ferments lactose to lactic acid
examFacts.importantDisease: Not a significant human pathogen — industrial dairy starter culture
examFacts.importantTest: Catalase test (negative); non-hemolytic on blood agar
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: The lactic acid bacterium behind cheese and buttermilk fermentation, formerly classified as Streptococcus lactis
